body: Outside a church, before five in the morning, two men are standing on the pavement because the building is full. It is cold enough that one of them is holding his coffee against his chest rather than drinking it. Inside, a chant has been going for some time and will be going for some time yet — slow, unhurried, carried on a drum and a rattle and a great many voices that are making no attempt whatever to blend. From the pavement it comes out through the propped doors in waves, thins away, comes back. The younger of the two has been awake since three. He is not fasting well and he knows it. He stays where he is.

A visitor standing beside him on that pavement would almost certainly reach for the word ancient, and would mean it as a compliment about the sound. It is not a description of the sound. It is a description of the fact.

Ethiopia was Christian as a kingdom in the fourth century, well before most of Europe. The Ethiopian Church has been developing its own worship continuously ever since, and it did not develop it by way of the West.

Take continuously literally, because that is the whole of the claim. This is not a revival of something, not a reconstruction worked up out of manuscripts, and not an archaism adopted for effect the way a Western group might reach for plainchant to signal depth. It is a line that never broke. It has its own hymnody, ascribed by the tradition to Yared; its own written notation, developed for its own chant and read by the people who sing it; its own liturgical language in Ge’ez; and its own instruments, including a large lyre, a drum and a hand-held rattle, none of which arrived from anywhere else. Set beside the history of European church music it is not a variant of it. It is a parallel line that happens to be older.

The frequency for it exists on this dial and it is silent. HM 331.50 Ethiopia Inspire (አማርኛ) is held, is still in build, and has no audio on it yet — which means you can read about it here this evening and you cannot listen to it.

Holding a number open before there is anything to put on it is the costly way of doing this, and in this case it is also the only respectful one. A tradition like this cannot be assembled by licensing a handful of tracks and calling the result a station. It needs somebody who knows the calendar and the fasts, the order of the year, which recordings are the ones people actually keep and which are the ones nobody plays twice. That takes as long as it takes and it cannot be hurried by wanting it. This is not an old-sounding style. It is an old style, developed continuously, that simply never passed through anybody else’s hands, and there is no shortcut to putting it on the air properly.

The framing it usually receives is the real problem. Ethiopian sacred music tends to arrive in the West filed under world music, a shelf defined entirely by what it is not, and the compliment it is paid is almost always about texture — how haunting it is, how atmospheric, how well it sits under a documentary. Underneath that sits an assumption so widespread it is rarely said out loud: that Christianity arrived in Africa with the colonial period, and that anything both Christian and African is therefore recent and derivative. In a good deal of the continent the faith had been there for well over a thousand years by the time anybody turned up to introduce it.

This has consequences for how such a station has to be programmed. It cannot be run as a sequence of pleasant excerpts, because the material is not built in three-minute units in the first place; a chant is long because the thing it is doing takes that long to do. The station has to be allowed to run at its own speed, which is slower than the rest of the dial and a great deal slower than an ear trained on choruses will expect for the first quarter of an hour.
The usual alternative is to take a melody like this and arrange it — strings, a pad, a tasteful producer, a runtime under four minutes. It is not a crime. It is a substitution.

And it can be genuinely beautiful. Some of those arrangements have been made with real love by musicians who knew exactly what they were handling, and they have carried something into rooms that would never otherwise have heard a note of it. But an arrangement makes a series of decisions on the listener’s behalf. It smooths the intonation towards the tuning system the listener already has. It evens out the rhythm. It shortens the whole thing to a length that will not test anybody. Each of those is a small mercy, and together they remove the reason the music exists. What made it worth hearing was never the exotic surface. It was that the people who built it were answering a different set of questions.
You cannot make it easier to listen to without making it something else.

A woman of thirty-four is packing up her grandmother’s flat, because her grandmother is moving into the spare room and has refused all help with any part of it. In a drawer under the television there are cassettes with nothing written on the labels. Finding a machine that will play them takes most of an afternoon and two phone calls to an uncle. She puts one on with no expectation of any kind. What comes out is her grandmother, decades younger, and a room full of people, and a chant she has heard her entire life without once wondering where it came from or how old it might be. She listens to both sides of the tape. Her grandmother comes in near the end of it, looks at the machine, says the name of the deacon who is leading, and goes to put the kettle on.

Nothing in that afternoon required anybody to explain a tradition to her. She had been inside it since she was small. What she had never had was any particular reason to notice that it ran back a very long way behind her grandmother.

The honest cost of a station like this is that it asks for a patience you may not have got. If your ear was formed on four-bar phrases and a chorus arriving in the second minute, the first stretch of Ethiopian chant will feel like waiting for something. Nothing turns up when you expect it to. The intonation will sound faintly out — it is not out; it is a different system, and the fault is in your expectations rather than in the singing. Knowing that does not make the first fifteen minutes any shorter.

That difficulty is not an obstacle standing in front of the music. It is an accurate description of what happens whenever anybody meets a thing that was not made with them in mind, and it is worth a good deal. A dial that only ever plays what your ear has already been trained on will confirm you and will never enlarge you. Fifteen difficult minutes is a very small tuition fee for discovering that what you had taken to be the mainstream of Christian music is one tributary of it, and not the oldest.

So the claim is precise. Ethiopian worship does not sound ancient because somebody chose an antique aesthetic for it. It sounds like that because it is old and it never stopped, and because it was never routed through the European and American sources that virtually everything else on international Christian radio is downstream of. It is one of the small number of places on earth where you can hear what Christian music sounds like when it was not standing on the same shelf as everything else.
The Amharic frequency is not playing yet, so the useful question is where else on this dial the same thing is true tonight.

There are 40 international stations here across 29 languages, and most of them, honestly, are downstream in the way just described — well made, properly hosted, local in language, and still working inside a harmonic world that came from somewhere else. That is not a criticism of them; it is simply what the last century did to church music everywhere. The exceptions are worth knowing by number, because they are the places where you can hear a tradition that took a different road out of the first few centuries and never rejoined the main one.

The nearest of those you can put on tonight is HM 329.00 — Israel Inspire (עברית), which is on air. Hebrew worship is not Ethiopian worship and the two should not be blurred into one another. But it shares the property that matters for this argument: it is sung in a language that was carrying these texts long before there was any such thing as Western hymnody, in the names the Scriptures actually use, and it is hosted rather than translated. Listen for the same things you would listen for in Amharic — phrase lengths that decline to resolve where you expect, ornament that is structural rather than decorative, a settled relationship between a text and a melody that was worked out a very long time ago by people who were not consulting anybody in Europe.

There is nothing to install and no card to hand over. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays — the whole thing is built for inexpensive handsets and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have rather than the hardware a launch video assumes. If you want it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else there. And do make an account while you are on it. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for — which is how the ones still in build get moved up the queue.

So give it the fifteen minutes rather than a verdict. Put it on while you are doing something with your hands, let the first stretch be strange, and stay past the point where you would normally have reached for something more familiar. That is the entire discipline being asked for here, and it is the same discipline the men on the pavement were exercising at five in the morning in the cold. Nobody in that doorway was being entertained either. They were staying, because the thing going on inside was older than their preferences and would still be going on after them.
